title: Marina Rice
text:
BIODIVERSITY · ECOLOGICAL DATA · GEOSPATIAL VISUALIZATION
An interactive exploration of biodiversity observations in Key Largo, using ecological occurrence data to examine species patterns across a climate-sensitive ecosystem.

Python GBIF Folium Geospatial Data

View on GitHub ← Back to Projects




EcoScope is a Python-based biodiversity visualization project exploring approximately a decade of species observations in the Key Largo area.
The project uses biodiversity occurrence records from GBIF to examine where species have been observed and to transform those records into an interactive geographic visualization.
The goal was to make ecological observation data easier to explore while connecting computational analysis with my broader interest in conservation and biodiversity.



Biodiversity databases contain large numbers of individual species observations collected across different locations and time periods.
When viewed as rows in a dataset, it can be difficult to understand how those observations relate to the landscape in which they were recorded.
EcoScope explores how geospatial visualization can provide additional context by placing biodiversity observations back onto the geographic environment they represent.

The project combines programmatic biodiversity data access with Python-based processing and interactive geospatial visualization.







I used Python to work with biodiversity occurrence data from GBIF and prepare relevant species, location, and observation information for visualization.
Folium was used to translate geographic coordinates into an interactive map, allowing biodiversity records to be explored spatially rather than only through tabular data.
The project provided an opportunity to combine biological data, programmatic data access, and geospatial visualization within a single workflow.



EcoScope also connects my computational work with my interest in conservation and ecological monitoring.
My previous conservation experience has included wildlife monitoring, vegetation surveys, habitat restoration, GPS-supported field activities, and community-science projects in Southern California.
Working with biodiversity occurrence data provided another perspective on the same broader challenge: transforming individual biological observations into structured information that can support exploration and interpretation.



This project strengthened my experience working with biological data outside of human genomics and introduced additional considerations involved in ecological and geospatial datasets.
I gained practice retrieving and processing biodiversity records, working with geographic coordinates, and building interactive maps with Python and Folium.
It also reinforced my interest in applying computational methods across different areas of biology, including biodiversity informatics and conservation data.

text:
CFDE DATA VISUALIZATION CHALLENGE · 3RD PLACE
An interactive spatial-biology visualization exploring cell populations within HuBMAP lymph node tissue.

Python Streamlit Plotly HuBMAP

View on GitHub ← Back to Projects




This project was developed for the CFDE Data Visualization Challenge using HuBMAP lymph node data.
The goal was to make complex spatial biological data easier to explore by transforming cell-center and cluster information into an interactive 3D visualization.
The project placed 3rd overall in the challenge.



Spatial biology datasets contain information not only about which cell types are present, but also about where those cells are located relative to one another.
Visualizing those relationships can help reveal tissue organization and patterns that may be difficult to understand from tables alone.
This project focused on creating an intuitive way to explore the spatial organization of cell populations within lymph node tissue.





01




INPUT HuBMAP Lymph Node Data


↓



Cell Centers Spatial coordinates


Clusters Cell population labels



↓


OUTPUT Interactive 3D Tissue View



Cell-center coordinates and cluster information were combined to represent tissue organization in three dimensions.

Data processing

Prepared and structured spatial data for visualization.




PLOTLY

3D visualization

Rendered interactive spatial plots for exploring cell populations.




STREAMLIT

Interactive interface

Provided an accessible environment for exploring the visualization.





The project combined Python-based data handling with interactive scientific visualization tools.

4

The visualization translated structured spatial data into an interactive representation of tissue architecture.




04




Area Approach Result


Data HuBMAP spatial biology 3D exploration


Tools Python + Plotly Interactive visualization


Challenge CFDE 3rd Place



The final visualization was recognized with 3rd place in the CFDE Data Visualization Challenge.







I used Python to work with cell-center and cluster data and Plotly to represent the spatial organization of cell populations in three dimensions.
Streamlit provided the interactive application layer, allowing the visualization to be explored more intuitively than a static figure.
The project emphasized scientific communication as much as technical implementation: the goal was to make a complex biological dataset easier to investigate visually.



This project strengthened my skills in biological data visualization and reinforced the importance of choosing representations that help users understand complex scientific datasets.
I gained additional experience working with spatial biological data, interactive Plotly visualizations, and Streamlit application development.
It also strengthened my interest in scientific computing tools that make high-dimensional biological data easier to explore.

title: Marina Rice
text:
Where Biology Meets Data
I’m a clinical genomics professional and M.S. Bioinformatics student building toward a career in bioinformatics and computational biology.
At GeneDx, I work with high-throughput genetic testing workflows across whole genome sequencing, whole exome sequencing, microarray, mitochondrial, repeat expansion, and reanalysis cases. This experience has given me a strong appreciation for data quality, reproducibility, and careful interpretation in clinical genomics.
Alongside my work, I’m developing computational skills through Python-based genomics projects, bioinformatics coursework, collaborative technical programs, and biological data visualization. I’m especially interested in genomic data analysis, scientific computing, and computational approaches that connect biological questions with reproducible analysis.

title: Marina Rice
text:
DECODE INSTITUTE · 1ST PLACE CAPSTONE
A team research project investigating shared extracellular RNA biomarkers across neurodegenerative and cognitive disorders.

Bioinformatics R DESeq2 Biological Interpretation

← Back to Projects




The DeCoDE Institute capstone focused on identifying shared extracellular RNA signals across neurodegenerative and cognitive disorders.
Our team explored patterns across multiple biological datasets and worked to interpret potential biomarker signals within the broader disease context.
The project placed 1st overall in the capstone program.



My primary role focused on biological research and interpretation.
I reviewed disease biology and relevant literature to help contextualize computational findings, support team discussions, and strengthen the biological interpretation presented in the final project.
I also explored differential expression analysis with DESeq2 using one project dataset as additional hands-on practice.



The project investigated whether extracellular RNA biomarkers could reveal biological signals shared across multiple neurodegenerative and cognitive conditions.
Extracellular RNA is particularly interesting because it may provide measurable molecular information outside of cells and has potential applications in biomarker discovery.
Our work centered on connecting computational findings with biologically meaningful interpretations.

Investigated whether multiple neurological and cognitive conditions showed overlapping extracellular RNA patterns.

The project combined computational analysis, biological research, and collaborative interpretation and received 1st place.







This project strengthened my ability to connect computational findings with biological context rather than treating analytical results in isolation.
I gained experience working within a collaborative research team, evaluating biological relevance, communicating scientific interpretations, and thinking more critically about how molecular signals may relate across complex disorders.
My independent DESeq2 practice also gave me additional exposure to differential expression workflows and interpretation.



This capstone was completed collaboratively as part of the DeCoDE Institute program. My contribution focused on biological research and interpretation supporting the team’s analysis and final presentation.

title: Marina Rice
text:
UC SAN DIEGO EXTENDED STUDIES · BIOINFORMATICS FUNDAMENTALS
A rule-based workflow integrating BLAST, HMMER, and TMHMM evidence to assign functional annotations to unknown genomic sequences.

Python BLAST HMMER TMHMM

View on GitHub ← Back to Projects




Functional annotation often requires combining evidence from multiple bioinformatics tools, each providing a different type of biological information.
This project explored how sequence similarity, conserved protein domains, and transmembrane predictions could be integrated into a consistent annotation workflow.
The pipeline uses outputs from BLAST, HMMER, and TMHMM and applies a rule-based hierarchy to determine the most appropriate functional annotation for each sequence.





01




INPUT Unknown Sequence


↓



HMMER Protein domains


BLAST Sequence similarity


TMHMM Membrane topology



↓


INTEGRATION Evidence Comparison


↓


DECISION Rule-Based Logic


↓


OUTPUT Functional Annotation



BLAST, HMMER, and TMHMM provide complementary biological evidence that is evaluated through a structured annotation workflow.




02




HMMER

Conserved protein domains

Identifies protein-family and domain-level evidence.




BLAST

Sequence similarity

Compares unknown sequences with known biological sequences.




TMHMM

Membrane topology

Predicts transmembrane regions that may support functional interpretation.





Each analysis method contributes a different type of biological evidence to the annotation process.




03




1

Evaluate available bioinformatics evidence






2

Compare results across analysis methods






3

Apply predefined annotation rules






4

Assign the most supported functional annotation




A rule-based hierarchy converts multiple analysis outputs into a consistent annotation decision.




04




Sequence Evidence Annotation


SEQ_01 HMMER + BLAST Functional assignment


SEQ_02 TMHMM Membrane-associated protein


SEQ_03 Limited evidence Unresolved / hypothetical



Representative layout showing how computational evidence is translated into final functional annotations.







Different bioinformatics tools capture different biological signals.
BLAST can identify sequence similarity to known sequences, HMMER can detect conserved protein domains, and TMHMM can predict transmembrane topology.
A major challenge is determining how to interpret these results together when the evidence does not point to a single obvious annotation.



I designed a rule-based decision hierarchy that combines evidence from each analysis method.
The workflow evaluates available evidence and prioritizes stronger biological signals before assigning a final functional annotation.

Unknown Sequence
↓
BLAST · HMMER · TMHMM
↓
Evidence Comparison
↓
Rule-Based Decision Hierarchy
↓
Functional Annotation




The workflow was implemented in Python and structured around outputs produced by BLAST, HMMER, and TMHMM.
The annotation logic compares available evidence and applies predefined rules to determine which result should guide the final assignment.
This approach helped make the annotation process more consistent and reproducible than interpreting each tool result independently.



The final workflow produced functional annotations by integrating multiple forms of bioinformatics evidence within a single decision framework.
The project demonstrated how complementary analysis tools can be combined to create a structured annotation process rather than relying on one source of evidence alone.



This project strengthened my understanding of how bioinformatics tools can be combined within a larger computational workflow.
I gained additional experience working with biological sequence-analysis outputs, translating scientific reasoning into Python logic, and designing a reproducible process for interpreting multiple sources of evidence.



The complete project implementation and documentation are available on GitHub.
